title: Socially constructed or physiologically informed? Placing humans at the core of understanding cooling needs
review_question: To expand the understanding of thermal comfort beyond a dominant technical focus and examine the broader, largely underutilized, literature on material culture, everyday practices, and sociocultural influences on how a range of human factors influence people's preferences for cooling thermal comfort, by placing humans and their physiological interactions with space, culture, and society at the center of investigation.
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Studies from social science and humanities fields (sociology, experimental psychology, sensory anthropology, material culture, geographies of consumption, architecture, design, neuro-architecture) that examine thermal comfort with particular attention to cooling, focusing on human-centric and social aspects, and excluding purely technical perspectives on cooling thermal comfort.

synthesis_conclusions: Cooling needs and preferences are grounded in both cultural and corporeal perceptions, resulting from individual subjective experience of external stimuli within the body, culture, space, and society.
Placing humans at the core of understanding the origins of cooling needs is key to enabling a more sustainable cooling future.
Thermal comfort is a socio-cultural human construction, influenced by the body, mind, space, and broader society/culture, and goes beyond simple heat-exchange models.

Assessing thermal comfort from a human-centric perspective and navigating different ontological positions is crucial for understanding cooling needs and broadening the focus from technology-driven to cultural-behavioural cooling solutions.
evidence_gaps: More work is needed to explore how differentiated skills and embodied activities interact with thermal adaptability and human metabolism.
More work is needed to better understand the 'thermal memories' of cooling.

There is little discussion about what types of food and drinks people consume to achieve cooling outcomes across different geographies, and the effects of regionally specific diets on overall thermal comfort are largely ignored.
There is little work on how language differences (e.g., limited adjectives to describe thermal sensations) influence how people describe and feel about thermal comfort.
It is unclear whether menthol activates skin thermoceptors and effectively lowers skin temperature, or if it merely desensitizes warm receptors.
Additional literature on the intersections between emotions and thermal comfort is needed for understanding thermal comfort and energy consumption beyond heat-exchange models.
More attention is needed on the impact of accumulated behavioural strategies ('cooling stacking') and their contribution to passive cooling and carbon mitigation.

Further work is needed on how networks of agents (institutions, firms, standard agencies, policy-makers, consumers) create and reproduce collective conventions around thermal comfort, and the influence of new popular social media on thermal comfort, design, and cooling technologies.
limitations: The review is cognizant of the limitations of the search and of inadvertent omissions which further work and systematic topic modelling can help identify.
